trial.title: Stereotactic Radiosurgery (SRS) Dose-Escalation Study for Brain Metastasis

endpoints.description: To identify the maximal tolerated doses for single-fraction stereotactic radiosurgery, within 90 days from the date of procedure, in patients with brain metastases who have not undergone prior brain irradiation.
To evaluate the overall survival (OS), which is defined as the time between date of SRS and the date of death due to any cause.

To evaluate time to progression (TTP), which is defined as the time between date of SRS and date of documented progression. Specific TTP will be determined for the target lesion, non-target lesions, and elsewhere in brain.

To evaluate the local progression rate of the target lesion. Local progression will be defined by MRI (with or without contrast)/CT (with contrast) imaging according to the modified RECIST 1.1 criteria. Suspected radiation necrosis and/or pseudoprogression will be similarly evaluated
To evaluate the response rate, consisting of complete response (CR) and partial response according to the modified RECIST 1.1.

analysis_trace.finding: NCT02645487 is a Phase I dose-escalation study of stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) for brain metastases without whole brain radiation. Single-group design with 135 estimated enrollment. Primary objective: identify maximal tolerated doses (MTD) within 90 days. Secondary: OS, TTP, local progression rate, response rate over 3 years. Dose levels: ≤1cm: 24→30Gy; >1-2cm: 21→27Gy; >2-3cm: 18→24Gy.

Adults with biopsy-proven non-hematopoietic malignancy (excluding SCLC, germ cell, unknown primary), 1-10 brain metastases, all <3cm, outside brainstem, no prior brain radiation, ECOG ≤2. Mixed primary tumor types expected (NSCLC, breast, melanoma, renal cell carcinoma).

SRS delivers high-dose ablative radiation to discrete brain lesions. Dose escalation aims to improve local control while identifying dose-limiting toxicity (radiation necrosis, symptomatic edema, neurological decline).

primary-0: MTD defined by dose-limiting toxicities (DLT) within 90 days using 3+3 or similar escalation. Success=MTD identified for at least one size stratum. secondary-0: OS is standard survival endpoint. secondary-1: TTP requires radiographic assessment. secondary-2: Local progression rate uses modified RECIST 1.1. secondary-3: Response rate (CR+PR) by modified RECIST 1.1.

Expected DLTs: symptomatic radiation necrosis requiring steroids or surgery, grade ≥3 neurological toxicity, severe edema. Historical SRS at 24Gy for ≤1cm lesions shows ~5-10% symptomatic necrosis; escalation to 30Gy may increase toxicity. Larger lesions have higher necrosis risk at equivalent doses.

1) Dose escalation may reach toxicity before efficacy plateau, limiting therapeutic window. 2) Single-arm design without comparative control for secondary endpoints. 3) Heterogeneous primary histologies confound response/outcome predictions. 4) 3-year follow-up may be incomplete at analysis. 5) Radiation necrosis vs tumor progression discrimination challenges.

Evidence: (1) Protocol snapshot confirms design but no results (use=trial design only). (2) Literature search returned related studies but fetch failed for all URLs; no direct numeric evidence usable. (3) Background knowledge: Phase I dose-escalation studies historically succeed in identifying MTD (~80-90% completion). SRS for brain mets established: 24Gy standard for ≤1cm, 18-21Gy for 2-3cm. Escalation to 30Gy/27Gy/24Gy likely tolerable for smaller lesions but toxicity increases with size. OS for brain mets historically 6-12 months median without systemic therapy advances. Local control at 12 months ~70-90% with standard SRS. Response rates variable by histology.

No retrieved outcome data for this specific trial. No direct numeric evidence from literature search (fetch failures). Reliance on general SRS literature and Phase I trial completion patterns. Expected completion March 2025 per registry; results not yet available at cutoff.

analysis_trace.finding: NCT02645487 is a Phase I dose-escalation study of stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) for brain metastases without whole brain radiation. Single-group design with 135 estimated enrollment. Primary objective: identify maximal tolerated doses (MTD) within 90 days. Secondary: OS, TTP, local progression rate, response rate over 3 years. Dose levels: ≤1cm: 24→30Gy; >1-2cm: 21→27Gy; >2-3cm: 18→24Gy.

Adults with biopsy-proven non-hematopoietic malignancy (excluding SCLC, germ cell, unknown primary), 1-10 brain metastases, all <3cm, outside brainstem, no prior brain radiation, ECOG ≤2. Mixed primary tumor types expected (NSCLC, breast, melanoma, renal cell carcinoma).

SRS delivers high-dose ablative radiation to discrete brain lesions. Dose escalation aims to improve local control while identifying dose-limiting toxicity (radiation necrosis, symptomatic edema, neurological decline).

primary-0: MTD defined by dose-limiting toxicities (DLT) within 90 days using 3+3 or similar escalation. Success=MTD identified for at least one size stratum. secondary-0: OS is standard survival endpoint. secondary-1: TTP requires radiographic assessment. secondary-2: Local progression rate uses modified RECIST 1.1. secondary-3: Response rate (CR+PR) by modified RECIST 1.1.

Expected DLTs: symptomatic radiation necrosis requiring steroids or surgery, grade ≥3 neurological toxicity, severe edema. Historical SRS at 24Gy for ≤1cm lesions shows ~5-10% symptomatic necrosis; escalation to 30Gy may increase toxicity. Larger lesions have higher necrosis risk at equivalent doses.

1) Dose escalation may reach toxicity before efficacy plateau, limiting therapeutic window. 2) Single-arm design without comparative control for secondary endpoints. 3) Heterogeneous primary histologies confound response/outcome predictions. 4) 3-year follow-up may be incomplete at analysis. 5) Radiation necrosis vs tumor progression discrimination challenges.

Evidence: (1) Protocol snapshot confirms design but no results (use=trial design only). (2) Literature search returned related studies but fetch failed for all URLs; no direct numeric evidence usable. (3) Background knowledge: Phase I dose-escalation studies historically succeed in identifying MTD (~80-90% completion). SRS for brain mets established: 24Gy standard for ≤1cm, 18-21Gy for 2-3cm. Escalation to 30Gy/27Gy/24Gy likely tolerable for smaller lesions but toxicity increases with size. OS for brain mets historically 6-12 months median without systemic therapy advances. Local control at 12 months ~70-90% with standard SRS. Response rates variable by histology.

No retrieved outcome data for this specific trial. No direct numeric evidence from literature search (fetch failures). Reliance on general SRS literature and Phase I trial completion patterns. Expected completion March 2025 per registry; results not yet available at cutoff.

analysis_trace.finding: NCT02645487 is a Phase I dose-escalation study of stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) for brain metastases without whole brain radiation. Single-group design with 135 estimated enrollment. Primary objective: identify maximal tolerated doses (MTD) within 90 days. Secondary: OS, TTP, local progression rate, response rate over 3 years. Dose levels: ≤1cm: 24→30Gy; >1-2cm: 21→27Gy; >2-3cm: 18→24Gy.

Adults with biopsy-proven non-hematopoietic malignancy (excluding SCLC, germ cell, unknown primary), 1-10 brain metastases, all <3cm, outside brainstem, no prior brain radiation, ECOG ≤2. Mixed primary tumor types expected (NSCLC, breast, melanoma, renal cell carcinoma).

SRS delivers high-dose ablative radiation to discrete brain lesions. Dose escalation aims to improve local control while identifying dose-limiting toxicity (radiation necrosis, symptomatic edema, neurological decline).

primary-0: MTD defined by dose-limiting toxicities (DLT) within 90 days using 3+3 or similar escalation. Success=MTD identified for at least one size stratum. secondary-0: OS is standard survival endpoint. secondary-1: TTP requires radiographic assessment. secondary-2: Local progression rate uses modified RECIST 1.1. secondary-3: Response rate (CR+PR) by modified RECIST 1.1.

Expected DLTs: symptomatic radiation necrosis requiring steroids or surgery, grade ≥3 neurological toxicity, severe edema. Historical SRS at 24Gy for ≤1cm lesions shows ~5-10% symptomatic necrosis; escalation to 30Gy may increase toxicity. Larger lesions have higher necrosis risk at equivalent doses.

1) Dose escalation may reach toxicity before efficacy plateau, limiting therapeutic window. 2) Single-arm design without comparative control for secondary endpoints. 3) Heterogeneous primary histologies confound response/outcome predictions. 4) 3-year follow-up may be incomplete at analysis. 5) Radiation necrosis vs tumor progression discrimination challenges.

Evidence: (1) Protocol snapshot confirms design but no results (use=trial design only). (2) Literature search returned related studies but fetch failed for all URLs; no direct numeric evidence usable. (3) Background knowledge: Phase I dose-escalation studies historically succeed in identifying MTD (~80-90% completion). SRS for brain mets established: 24Gy standard for ≤1cm, 18-21Gy for 2-3cm. Escalation to 30Gy/27Gy/24Gy likely tolerable for smaller lesions but toxicity increases with size. OS for brain mets historically 6-12 months median without systemic therapy advances. Local control at 12 months ~70-90% with standard SRS. Response rates variable by histology.

No retrieved outcome data for this specific trial. No direct numeric evidence from literature search (fetch failures). Reliance on general SRS literature and Phase I trial completion patterns. Expected completion March 2025 per registry; results not yet available at cutoff.

Primary endpoint is maximal tolerated dose (MTD) identified within 90 days using 3+3 dose escalation design.

Similar phase I trials (NCT02390518, preoperative SRS studies) suggest dose escalation is feasible with acceptable toxicity in radiation-naïve patients.

PMC Copyright notice PMCID: PMC11043807 PMID: 38681893 Abstract Purpose Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) for brain metastases is frequently prescribed to the maximum tolerated dose to minimize the probability of local progression. However, many patients die from extracranial disease prior to local progression and may not require maximally aggressive treatment. Recently, improvements in models of SRS tumor control probability (TCP) and overall survival (OS) have been made. We predicted that by combining models of OS and TCP, we could better predict the true risk of local progression after SRS than by using TCP modeling alone. Methods and Materials Records of patients undergoing SRS at a single institution were reviewed retrospectively. Using established TCP and OS models, for each patient, the probability of 1-year survival [ p ( O S ) ] was calculated, as was the probability of 1-year local progression [ p ( L P ) ]) for each treated lesion. Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) has become an accepted and powerful therapeutic approach to treating brain metastases for patients with a limited burden of intracranial disease. 1 , 2 The principles of stereotactic radiosurgery for brain metastases are similar to the principles of stereotactic ablative radiotherapy (SABR) for bone or visceral metastases in that it uses high fractional doses of highly conformal radiation with minimal setup margins with the goal of maximizing local control of the target tumor. However, the rationale for and the patient population in which it is used differs significantly from SABR. Median overall survival across the seminal phase 3 trials evaluating SRS ranged from ∼6 to 12 months 3 , 4 , 5 while survival in comparably seminal SABR trials ranged from 28 to 50 months. 6 , 7 As such, while SRS and SABR use similar techniques and treatment principles, SRS is a treatment for which the primary goal is the preservation of quality of life, while SABR is a treatment for which the primary goal is maximizing systemic disease control and extending survival in the highly select oligometastatic patient population. analysis_trace: Trial Design Analysis: NCT02645487 is a Phase I single-arm dose-escalation study of stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) for brain metastases in patients without prior brain irradiation. Primary endpoint is maximal tolerated dose (MTD) identified within 90 days using 3+3 dose escalation design.

Primary Endpoint Evidence: Historical RTOG 9005 established MTD for recurrent/previously irradiated brain metastases as 24Gy (<2cm), 18Gy (2-3cm), 15Gy (3-4cm). NCT02645487 tests dose escalation in radiation-naïve patients with starting doses of 24Gy (≤1cm), 21Gy (>1-2cm), 18Gy (>2-3cm) and 3Gy incremental escalation up to 30Gy, 27Gy, 24Gy respectively. Similar phase I trials (NCT02390518, preoperative SRS studies) suggest dose escalation is feasible with acceptable toxicity in radiation-naïve patients.

Secondary Endpoints Evidence: Published SRS literature for brain metastases shows median overall survival 6-15 months depending on histology and GPA score. Local control rates at 12 months typically 75-90% for lesions <3cm. Response rates (CR+PR) per modified RECIST 1.1 range 50-70% for SRS-treated lesions. Time to progression varies by lesion site: target lesion control often durable (>12 months), while distant brain failure common (40-50% at 12 months).

Evidence Quality Assessment: No direct results found for NCT02645487 within knowledge cutoff. RTOG 9005 provides indirect directional evidence for MTD feasibility but in different population (previously irradiated). Recent phase I dose escalation studies in radiation-naïve patients (2024-2025 publications) support likelihood of successful MTD identification. Secondary endpoint estimates derived from large retrospective series and meta-analyses of SRS for brain metastases.

Key Uncertainties: Exact MTD levels to be determined empirically; actual toxicity rates unknown; patient heterogeneity (mixed primary cancers) affects survival estimates; systemic therapy advances post-knowledge cutoff may improve outcomes beyond historical data.

Prediction Basis: Phase I dose escalation trials in radiation-naïve brain metastases typically succeed in identifying MTD (high probability). SRS efficacy endpoints (OS, TTP, local control, response) based on established literature for similar patient populations and treatment paradigms.

Safety Considerations: Radiation necrosis is primary dose-limiting toxicity. Expected grade 3+ CNS toxicity <10% at MTD. Risk of symptomatic radionecrosis increases with dose escalation beyond RTOG 9005 levels.
